notes:
I've written notes for every verse I could support from pages I actually read. A few gaps up front:

- **Pages I couldn't reach:** the Enduring Word page was blocked, and I never reached the Catholic or Orthodox sites (catholic.com, newadvent.org, oca.org), bibleodyssey.org, any Pentecostal sites, or anything on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter.
- **Catholic reading:** the only Catholic voice I found is Haydock's older commentary on v. 26. The Catholic reading of v. 32 appears only as Protestant commentators describe and criticise it.
- **Thin verses:** vv. 29–31 and v. 33 have only light coverage.

## Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1:** The Pulpit Commentary links this verse to 4:32. We forgive because God forgave us, and as loved children we should copy our Father's forgiving love. These words are closely connected with the preceding. In Ephesians 4:32 he had urged the example of God in one very momentous matter; he now urges it in a more general sense. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ephesians/5.htm
The Expositor's Greek Testament says this is the only place in the New Testament where "imitator" is used of imitating God. Because we are God's children and experience His love, we should be like our Father. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/egt/ephesians-5.html

**v. 2:** Pulpit says "walk in love" picks up 4:1 again: ordinary life should be lived in an atmosphere of love. It reads "for us" as "in our place". It hears "sweet-smelling savour" as an echo of Noah's sacrifice: Christ's whole work, and the spirit in which He offered it, pleased the Father. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ephesians/5.htm
The Expositor's Greek Testament connects the "offering and sacrifice" language with Christ's death as a propitiation, that is, a sacrifice that removes guilt and restores fellowship with God. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/egt/ephesians-5.html

**v. 3:** Pulpit says Paul often pairs greed with sexual sin because, in his mind, sensual sin always craves more than is enough. Saints should not even make such sins a topic of ordinary talk. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ephesians/5.htm
The Expositor's Greek Testament notes that the Greco-Roman world had come to treat fornication as morally neutral. It also reports a debate over the word translated "greed": most take it as covetousness, while some take it as sexual greed. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/egt/ephesians-5.html

**v. 4:** Pulpit sees the target as frivolous banter full of double meanings and obscene hints. It says Paul is not condemning all humour, which is a Divine gift. Instead of joking, Christians should pour out their high spirits in thanks to God. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ephesians/5.htm
Matthew Henry's line is that Christians may be cheerful, but they must be merry and wise. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ephesians/5-5.html

**v. 5:** Pulpit calls greed the twin-brother sin of uncleanness, idolatry because it trusts in possessions rather than God. It also argues that naming Christ and God together implies Christ's divinity. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ephesians/5-5.htm and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ephesians/5.htm
Calvin says Paul used this frightening warning so readers would not treat his admonitions carelessly. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ephesians/5-5.html

**v. 6:** Matthew Henry says the "empty words" are flattery suggesting such sins are tolerable in Christians, or can be indulged without consequence. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eph/Eph_005.cfm
Pulpit identifies two sources: pagans defending a life of pleasure, and nominal Christians excusing "pleasant sins". It says God's wrath comes now and in the life to come. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ephesians/5.htm

**v. 7:** Pulpit: if you share their sins, you will share their punishment, so refuse any partnership. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ephesians/5.htm

**v. 8:** Pulpit stresses that Paul says the readers *were* darkness and *are* light, not merely that they were in it. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ephesians/5.htm
JFB puts the emphasis on "were": that state is now past. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Eph/Eph_005.cfm

**v. 9:** There is a manuscript difference here. Clarke reports that many early manuscripts and versions read "fruit of the light" rather than "of the Spirit", and most critics accept "light". — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ephesians/5-9.html
Pulpit defines the three fruits: goodness (a disposition to do good), righteousness (giving everyone their due) and truth (sincerity). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ephesians/5.htm

**v. 10:** Pulpit says "test" means finding out by trial what pleases Christ, rather than following custom or a vague sense of duty. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ephesians/5.htm

**v. 11:** Pulpit says the key word is "fruitless": dark deeds yield nothing good except shame. Christians should go beyond avoiding them and actively expose them. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ephesians/5.htm
Matthew Henry says such works come from the darkness of ignorance, look for concealment, and lead to hell. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eph/Eph_005.cfm

**v. 12:** Matthew Henry thinks Paul may mean the pagan "mysteries" with their secret wickedness. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ephesians/5-5.html
Pulpit points to Ephesus's notorious groves. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ephesians/5.htm

**v. 13:** Pulpit's example is Christ exposing the Pharisees: a just rebuke shows evil for what it really is. It adds that gospel light *tends* to transform what it shines on, though not always. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ephesians/5.htm

**v. 14:** Pulpit says no Old Testament verse matches these words; Isaiah 60:1 is closest. It thinks Paul gives the spirit of that passage rather than its exact words: the church, having received light, must wake up and shine on the world. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ephesians/5.htm

**v. 15:** Pulpit warns that some people are strict but not *wisely* strict. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ephesians/5.htm
Calvin pictures believers living as if in a crowded theatre, under the eyes of God and the angels. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ephesians/5-15.html

**v. 16:** Pulpit explains "redeeming the time" as a merchant buying up a valuable opportunity, here the chance to spread the light while evil prevails. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ephesians/5.htm

**v. 17:** Pulpit: the Lord's will is the great rule of Christian life. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ephesians/5.htm
The Light of Israel commentary goes further, suggesting a believer walking closely with God should already know His will. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ephesians/5-15.html

**v. 18:** Pulpit says Paul has drinking in company in view. Rather than wine, believers should open their hearts to the Spirit and express their joy in hymns instead of drinking songs. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ephesians/5.htm
Precept Austin contrasts this with the Dionysus cults, whose worshippers believed the god indwelt and controlled them. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/ephesians_518_commentary

**v. 19:** Pulpit admits the exact difference between "psalms, hymns and spiritual songs" is unclear. It suggests singing at social Christian gatherings, which by extension also belongs in public worship. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ephesians/5.htm

**v. 20:** Pulpit: give thanks always, and for all things, not only pleasant ones (it cites Job 2:10 and Romans 8:28). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ephesians/5.htm

**v. 21:** Bible.org says the literal sense is "submitting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ". It is the last of five participles that show the results of being filled with the Spirit. — https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-47-submitting-one-another-ephesians-521
Precept Austin says submitting does not mean being unequal, just as Christ submitted to the Father while remaining equal with Him. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/ephesians_521-22

**v. 22:** The Expositor's Greek Testament explains "as to the Lord" as meaning to Christ, not to the husband as lord and master. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/egt/ephesians-5.html

**v. 23:** Pulpit grounds headship in creation (Genesis 2:18; 1 Timothy 2:13). It notes that the parallel stops at Christ's saving work, which the husband does not share. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ephesians/5.htm

**v. 24:** The Expositor's Greek Testament reads the opening word as "nevertheless". Christ alone is Saviour, yet the wife's submission still follows the church's pattern. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/egt/ephesians-5.html

**v. 25:** Pulpit says Christlike love from the husband "restores the balance" and makes the wife's duty easy. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ephesians/5.htm
The Expositor's Greek Testament says this love must be ready to suffer and die for the wife. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/egt/ephesians-5.html
Both JFB and Barclay quote Chrysostom: if you want your wife to obey you as the church obeys Christ, care for her as Christ cares for the church. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Eph/Eph_005.cfm and https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ephesians/5-5.html

**v. 26:** Pulpit: Christ used the Word as the cleansing agent. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ephesians/5.htm
JFB compares it to a bride's purifying bath before marriage. — https://biblehub.com/m/ephesians/5-26.htm
(How this verse relates to baptism is debated; see the next section.)

**v. 27:** Pulpit says Christ both gives and receives the bride. The wedding comes in glory (Revelation 21:2), and this life is training for it. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ephesians/5.htm

**v. 28:** Calvin calls this an argument from nature: every man loves himself, so a man who does not love his wife is "a monster". — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ephesians/5-28.html
The Expositor's Greek Testament says this love comes from nature as well as duty. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/egt/ephesians-5.html

**v. 29:** The Light of Israel commentary quotes Hoehner: men care for their bodies even though they are imperfect, so they should care for imperfect wives. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ephesians/5-28.html

**v. 30:** JFB says the same love and bodily union exists between Christ and the church. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Eph/Eph_005.cfm

**v. 31:** Matthew Henry says marriage does not cancel a man's other family duties. It only puts this relationship ahead of all others, as the closest union. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eph/Eph_005.cfm

**v. 32:** Ellicott says marriage's sacredness is a "mystery" fully revealed only in Christ, but Paul's main thought moves on to Christ and the church. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ephesians/5-32.htm
GotQuestions says the mystery is not marriage itself but that God designed marriage to point to the gospel. — https://www.gotquestions.org/profound-mystery.html
Desiring God (Baptist): "mystery" here means a secret now made public, not something too deep to grasp. — https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/what-is-the-mystery-of-marriage

**v. 33:** Precept Austin: Paul brings readers back to ordinary home life, and "love his wife as himself" shows what kind of husband the wife is to submit to. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/ephesians_532-33

## Where traditions differ

**v. 18: Is being filled with the Spirit repeated?**
Baptist, Reformed and other evangelical voices agree it is ongoing, and some argue against a single "second experience":
- **Piper (Baptist):** being filled means great joy in God. He takes up the Pentecostal discussion and argues Spirit-filling is repeated, not once for all. — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/be-filled-with-the-spirit
- **MacArthur (gty.org):** filling means continual control by the Spirit, not a one-time "zap". — https://www.gty.org/sermons/1939/be-filled-with-the-spirit-part-1
- **Geoff Thomas (monergism.com, Reformed):** the grammar rules out a single definitive experience. — https://www.monergism.com/be-filled-spirit-eph-518
- **Expositor's Bible Commentary (quoted on Precept Austin):** there can be successive fillings, but the verse does not support one extra, definitive filling as necessary after conversion. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/ephesians_518_commentary

I found no Pentecostal source of its own to set against these.

**v. 21: Mutual submission?**
- **Egalitarian reading (as described by bible.org):** v. 21 is a controlling principle that removes gender-based hierarchy. — https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-47-submitting-one-another-ephesians-521
- **Complementarian reading, TGC (Kevin DeYoung):** "one another" means submitting to those over us (wives, children, slaves). — https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/complementarianism/
- **Complementarian reading, bible.org (Piper and Grudem's book):** offers both views: general mutual submission followed by the wife's specific duty, or a one-way reading. — https://bible.org/seriespage/8-husbands-and-wives-analogues-christ-and-church-ephesians-521-and-colossians-318-19
- **Themelios (TGC's journal), reviewing an egalitarian book:** describes that view, that "head" means "source", not authority. — https://media.thegospelcoalition.org/documents/themelios/Themelios-43-2.pdf

**v. 26: Is the "washing" baptism?**
- **Wesley (Methodist):** yes, it is baptism, if the inward grace is received with the outward sign. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ephesians/5-26.html
- **Calvin (Reformed):** baptism is the outward pledge of an inward cleansing, and he warns against turning a sacrament into an idol. — same page
- **Gill (Baptist):** it is not baptism at all, but Christ's blood. — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/niv/ephesians/5-26.html
- **Ellicott (Anglican):** the reference to baptism is "unquestionable". — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ephesians/5-26.htm
- I didn't get a page in the Lutheran tradition's own voice on this verse.

**v. 32: Is marriage a sacrament?**
- **Calvin, Barnes, Clarke and JFB:** they reject Rome's use of the Latin Vulgate's "great sacrament" here. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ephesians/5-32.html and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ephesians/5-32.htm
- **Ellicott:** the Latin rendering is where the habit of calling marriage a "sacrament" came from. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ephesians/5-32.htm
- **Barnes, unusually:** denies that marriage is even a type of Christ and the church. — same page
- **LCMS (Lutheran):** marriage is a mystery because it reflects God's love for His creation. — https://witness.lcms.org/2024/christ-and-the-church-ephesians-5-and-the-wonder-of-the-wedding-day/

## Other views

**v. 14, the quotation:** Pulpit says the words aren't found in the Old Testament. It takes them as Paul giving the gist of Isaiah 60:1. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ephesians/5.htm

**v. 18, NET Bible note:** it says many take the Greek phrase as "filled *with*", but the NET translates "filled *by* the Spirit": Christ fills believers by means of the Spirit with God's fullness. — https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Eph&chapter=5&verse=18

**v. 26 and v. 32, Catholic:**
- **Haydock (Catholic, 1811):** the washing is generally understood as the sacrament of baptism. Some take "word of life" as the words spoken at baptism, though he says this is "not so certain". — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ephesians/5-26.html
- **Douay-Rheims:** translates v. 32 as "a great sacrament". — https://biblehub.com/ephesians/5-32.htm
- **Meyer:** notes that Catholic scholars Cajetan and Estius themselves rejected using this verse to prove marriage is a sacrament. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ephesians/5-32.htm
